title: The Shepherd Who Discovered Coffee's Power
event_summary: In the mid-15th century, Sufi monks in Yemen's port city of Mocha began systematically roasting and brewing coffee beans — likely introduced from Ethiopian highlands — to sustain all-night prayer vigils called dhikr. A Yemeni scholar named Muhammad al-Dhabhani is credited in Arabic sources with popularizing the drink after observing its effects during his travels in Ethiopia. Within decades, Yemen established the world's first commercial coffee plantations on terraced mountainsides, and purpose-built coffeehouses called qahveh khaneh spread from Aden to Cairo to Constantinople, creating entirely new spaces for public intellectual exchange.
why_forgotten: European histories of coffee typically begin with Venetian merchants or Viennese cafés, erasing the century of Yemeni monopoly, Sufi spiritual practice, and Arab commercial infrastructure that made the global coffee trade possible. Yemen's later economic decline and colonial reframing cast the Arab world as a passive waypoint rather than coffee culture's deliberate architect.
why_it_matters: Yemen's coffeehouses became blueprints for the European cafés that fueled the Enlightenment, the French Revolution's planning, and London's insurance and stock markets. Coffee remains the world's second most traded commodity after oil, and the entire global stimulant economy — from Starbucks to energy drinks — traces directly to Sufi monks in Yemen who needed to stay awake to pray.
